items.followUp: How is text stored in a computer’s memory?

rubric.why: Identifies the binary form used to represent data in memory.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that memory represents data using binary digits or bits.

rubric.why: Shows what the binary digits represent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the two binary values.

modelAnswer: Computer memory represents data in binary form.
Each bit has one of two values: 0 or 1.

items.followUp: Give one example of volatile memory and one example of non-volatile memory.

rubric.why: States the defining behaviour of volatile memory.
rubric.description: Volatile memory loses its stored data when power is turned off.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that volatile memory does not retain data without power.

rubric.why: States the defining behaviour of non-volatile memory.
rubric.description: Non-volatile memory retains its data when power is turned off.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that non-volatile memory keeps data without power.

modelAnswer: Volatile memory loses its stored data when the power is switched off.
Non-volatile memory retains its stored data even when the power is switched off.

items.followUp: Write the base and digits used in the binary number system.

rubric.why: Identifies the base of the hexadecimal system.
rubric.description: Hexadecimal is a base-16 number system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that its base or radix is 16.

rubric.why: Identifies the symbols used to write hexadecimal numbers.
rubric.description: It uses digits 0–9 and letters A–F.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving both the decimal digits and the letters A through F.

modelAnswer: The hexadecimal number system has base 16.
It uses the digits 0–9 and the letters A–F to represent values.

items.followUp: Name two common types of software piracy.

rubric.why: Identifies a recognised type of software piracy.
rubric.description: One valid type of software piracy is named.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming one valid type, such as softlifting, hard-disk loading, counterfeiting or internet piracy.

rubric.why: Identifies another recognised type of software piracy.
rubric.description: A second valid type of software piracy is named.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a different valid type.

modelAnswer: Types of software piracy include softlifting, client-server overuse, hard-disk loading, counterfeiting and internet piracy.
Any two of these are examples of software piracy.

items.followUp: How can a computer virus be used to sabotage a computer system?

rubric.why: Shows that sabotage involves deliberate harm or disruption.
rubric.description: Sabotage is intentional damage or disruption.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the act is deliberate and harmful or disruptive.

rubric.why: Identifies what may be targeted by computer sabotage.
rubric.description: The harm is directed at a computer system, its data, network or equipment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a computer-related target.

modelAnswer: Sabotage is the intentional damage or disruption of a computer system.
It may involve damaging or destroying computer data, software or equipment.

items.followUp: What is one benefit of sharing files over a network?

rubric.why: Identifies the sharing or access of files as the central idea.
rubric.description: File sharing allows files to be accessed, exchanged or transferred.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing files being shared, accessed or transferred.

rubric.why: Identifies how or between whom files are shared.
rubric.description: Files are made available to users or computers through a network.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning a network or sharing between users/computers.

modelAnswer: File sharing is the process of making files available to other users or computers.
It is commonly done over a network so files can be accessed or transferred.

items.followUp: What is the role of the sender in data communication?

rubric.why: States that the receiver obtains the communicated information.
rubric.description: The receiver is the person or device that receives the message or data.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the receiver obtains the message or data.

rubric.why: Places the receiver in the communication process.
rubric.description: The receiver is the destination of data sent by a sender.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the receiver as the destination or other endpoint in data communication.

modelAnswer: In data communication, the receiver is the person or device that receives the message or data.
The receiver is the destination to which the sender transmits the information.

items.followUp: What is the main function of the Transport Layer in the OSI model?

rubric.why: Identifies the Application Layer’s position in the OSI model.
rubric.description: The Application Layer is the seventh and topmost layer of the OSI model.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as layer 7 or the topmost layer.

rubric.why: Describes the layer’s role in providing network functionality to applications or users.
rubric.description: It provides network services to applications and acts as an interface for users or application programs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing its provision of network services or its interface role.

modelAnswer: The Application Layer is the seventh and topmost layer of the OSI model.
It provides network services to application programs and serves as an interface between applications or users and the network.
